statement: A convex polygon has one interior angle of $90^\circ$, and every other interior angle is $150^\circ$. How many sides does the polygon have?

choices.misconception: I wrote the angle sum as $180(n-1)$ instead of $180(n-2)$, which gave $30(n-1) = 90$.
I found that nine angles of $150^\circ$ are needed but forgot to count the $90^\circ$ corner as a side too.
I worked out $(360 - 90) \div 30 = 9$ and then added 2, because the angle-sum formula has an $n - 2$ in it.
I ignored the $90^\circ$ angle and used a regular polygon with all angles $150^\circ$, which has 12 sides.

hints: Look at the angle outside each corner instead of inside it.
The exterior angles of any convex polygon add up to $360^\circ$. Turn each interior angle into its exterior angle, then count how many of each kind you need.
The $90^\circ$ corner has an exterior angle of $90^\circ$ and each $150^\circ$ corner has an exterior angle of $30^\circ$. So $90 + 30k = 360$, where $k$ is the number of $150^\circ$ corners.

solutions.reliable: Each exterior angle is $180^\circ$ minus the interior angle, so the polygon has one exterior angle of $90^\circ$ and the rest are $30^\circ$. Exterior angles of a convex polygon add up to $360^\circ$, so $90 + 30k = 360$, giving $k = 9$. With the $90^\circ$ corner the polygon has $9 + 1 = 10$ sides. Check with interior angles: $90 + 9 \times 150 = 1440 = 180 \times (10 - 2)$. The transferable idea: exterior angles always total $360^\circ$, which is often quicker than the interior-angle formula.
solutions.elegant: Using the interior sum directly: $90 + 150(n-1) = 180(n-2)$ gives $30n = 300$, so $n = 10$. The exterior-angle route avoids the algebra because $360^\circ$ does not depend on $n$.

whyOnTest: Exterior angles total $360^\circ$ for every convex polygon, a fixed number that turns a polygon with mixed angles into a one-line count.
